title: How to (Accidentally) Spot a Baku IT Guy. Tip #1
body: He works at Azercell, Kapital Bank, PASHA, or an outsourcing company nobody's heard of, and he will describe it as "a product company" either way. Ask what he does. If the answer is "backend" and nothing else, correct. If he says the salary out loud, he's lying or he's junior. Real ones say "normaldır." He did Code Academy or Step, not a university degree, and he will bring that up unprompted within nine minutes. Check the laptop stickers. Check whether the coffee at Coffee Moffie is his second or fourth. It's a sealed deal if he has an Estonian company registered for one client.

title: How to (Accidentally) Spot a Baku IT Guy. Tip #2
body: Ask what currency he's paid in. Manat is a job. Dollars is a career. Euro means he's already gone, he just hasn't told his mother. If he starts explaining the exchange rate unprompted, he's paid in dollars and wants you to know. Watch him at any restaurant when the bill comes, the dollar guy doesn't look. Ask about relocation. Poland, Germany, Netherlands, or Dubai, and each one comes with a cousin who already made it and sends voice notes about how the bread is worse. It's a sealed deal if his LinkedIn location says Baku but his timezone doesn't.

title: How to (Accidentally) Spot a Baku IT Guy. Tip #3
body: Look at the building. Port Baku Towers, Caspian Plaza, Hyatt Tower, AF Business House, that's the whole map. If he says "ofis Port Bakuda" the salary is fine. If the office is a converted apartment in Yasamal with three desks and one air conditioner, he's at a startup and hasn't been paid this month. If he works from home he'll tell you it's better and then describe his chair for four minutes. It's a sealed deal if he has been to the office twice this year and both times were for the New Year corporate.

title: How to (Accidentally) Spot a Baku IT Guy. Tip #4
body: Listen to the language. Azerbaijani with the security guard. Russian in the standup. English for every single technical noun, no exceptions, "deploy elədim," "merge eləmişəm," "bug var." Nobody has ever said any of these words in Azerbaijani and nobody ever will. If his mother asks what he does and he says "kompüterdə işləyirəm," that's the standard answer, everyone gives it, nobody has ever improved on it. It's a sealed deal if his grandmother still thinks he can fix her television.

title: How to (Accidentally) Spot a Baku IT Guy. Tip #5
body: Find out about military service. This is the real question and everyone dances around it. If he did it, he'll mention it constantly. If he deferred through university until 27, he will change the subject with impressive speed. If he did it in a warm office in Baku because someone made a phone call, that tells you what family he's from, which is a different conversation entirely. Ask casually. Watch the face. It's a sealed deal if the answer involves the word "təxirə" and a long pause.

title: How to (Accidentally) Spot a Baku IT Guy. Tip #6
body: Watch what happens on payday. The manat lands, and within two hours it's a PlayStation, a mechanical keyboard, or a monitor he does not need. Check his cart on Tap.az. Ask what he's saving for and the answer is a flat in a building that isn't built yet, on Ziya Bunyadov or out past Xırdalan, bought off a plan from a developer his uncle knows. Everyone is buying an unbuilt flat. Nobody has seen it. It's a sealed deal if he shows you the 3D render like it's a photograph.

title: How to (Accidentally) Spot a Baku IT Guy. Tip #7
body: Ask what he does after work. If it's the gym at 9pm and Boulevard after, he's fine. If it's freelance on Upwork until 3am for an American client who calls him "buddy," he's tired and rich. If it's a side project he's been building for two years and has never shown anyone, he's the most dangerous kind. Ask to see it. Watch him refuse. It's a sealed deal if he owns a domain name for a company that does not exist and renews it every year without fail.

title: How to (Accidentally) Spot a Baku IT Guy. Tip #8
body: Look at the phone. Latest iPhone bought in Dubai to skip the customs, or a Samsung he defends with genuine passion, there is no third option and the two groups do not speak. Check the AirPods, check whether they're real. Then check the car. A Prius means he is deeply practical and has done the maths. A Mercedes at 26 in IT means family money, because the salary does not do that, and everyone in the office already knows it. It's a sealed deal if he takes the metro to Nizami and the car stays parked at home.
